title: Image evidence: Mississippian (about 1000–1550 CE, western Kentucky)
summary: Maize-farming towns of western Kentucky with platform mounds, plazas and stockades, such as Wickliffe, Jonathan Creek and Tolu, and later Caborn-Welborn villages like Slack Farm.
displayNote: This picture is an AI illustration reconstructed from the available archaeological evidence for the Mississippian period in Kentucky; details without direct evidence are informed guesses. AI illustration · Kentucky History Drive. [Research notes](/research/culture-mississippian-image-evidence/)

items.text: Slack Farm forensic study counted at least 850 individuals, later reinterred; [Speculative] build and stature figures were not confirmed from open sources. Show ordinary farmers' builds.
Bone hair pins and pottery ear plugs, shell ear pins and copper or brass ear ornaments occur in Kentucky Mississippian and Caborn-Welborn graves.
[Speculative] Garments are not described in these sources; woven fiber and hide clothing is an inference. Fabric-impressed salt pans show textile use.
Engraved marine-shell gorgets (e.g. cross-and-circle and triskele designs), shell beads and ear plugs; cross-and-circle symbol painted on Wickliffe pottery.
Bow and small triangular arrow points; shell- and stone-bladed hoes; shell-tempered jars and bowls.
Bluffs and floodplains of the Mississippi, Ohio and Tennessee rivers; platform mounds around a plaza; bastioned stockades at Jonathan Creek; big corn-storage pits at Slack Farm.

A farmer on a bluff above the Mississippi–Ohio confluence, a flat-topped earthen mound and thatched houses around a plaza behind, wearing an engraved shell gorget with a cross-and-circle design and shell ear plugs, holding a hoe beside ripe corn. Hot humid floodplain light and wide brown rivers distinguish it from eastern settings.
